newsitem.title: USA: US Northeast power demand headed for a summer high.
newsitem.headline: US Northeast power demand headed for a summer high.

text.p: Hot, humid weather in the U.S. Northeast, accompanied by the incessant drone of air conditioners, is expected to send electricity demand across the region to its highest levels so far this summer.
Meteorologists have warned the temperature in New York City's Central Park is likely to hit 94 degrees Fahrenheit and hold at that level for the next few days.
"We certainly expect the load on our system to be high," said Joe Petta, a spokesman for Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc (ConEd).
Petta said the load on ConEd's system later today is forecast at 10,400 megawatts (MW), just 405 MW short of the 10,805 MW record hit August 2, 1995.
ConEd serves 2.9 million customers from Manhattan north to suburban Westchester County.
To help ease the strain, ConEd just brought back on line its 975 MW Indian Point 2 nuclear plant, which is ramping up power after being shut since May 14 for refueling.

Petta said this leaves ConEd with at least 18 percent reserve generation capacity, the cushion utilities in the New York Power Pool try to maintain to keep the power flowing in the event of a sudden outage at one or more of their plants.

The situation is a bit more precarious in the New England Power Pool (NEPOOL), which predicted a 19,800 MW peak load on its system Monday, cutting its operating reserve surplus to 839 MW, or only four percent of available generation capacity.

The slim backup reserves prompted NEPOOL to issue a "power caution", which flatly states that "although available supply of electricity...is sufficient to meet customer demand now, we do not have as much reserve on the system as we would like."
To avoid problems, NEPOOL is asking utilities across the six-state region to curtail non-emergency maintenance work.
"The main message we're trying to get out is: Don't do anything that might trip a unit or affect reliability on the transmission side," said NEPOOL spokesman Jim Sinclair.
NEPOOL coordinates operation of the power grid serving some 6.2 million New England customers.
Sinclair said the power caution was likely to last for the rest of the week, with NEPOOL load forecasts seen running between 19,500 and 20,000 MW through Friday.

Down in the Mid-Atlantic states, the operator of region's power grid said that despite high air conditioning demand, peak electricity usage will likely fall short of the record of 48,660 megawatts (MW) set in 1995.
The Pennsylvania-New Jersey-Maryland (PJM) Interconnect pool said power demand for Monday and Tuesday is expected to hit about 48,000 to 48,500 MW.
"We'll make it through the heatwave with sufficient (power) reserves," said PJM spoksman Jeff William.
Baltimore Gas and Electric Co said it did not expect to hit record peak electricity demand Monday despite forecasted highs near 100 degrees F.
A BG&E spokeswoman said peak demand this afternoon was likely to reach 5,700 MW, slightly less than the 5,917 MW seen on June 25.
BG&E's all-time peak demand was 5,947 MW, set on August 4, 1995.
((--J Jelter, New York Power Desk + 212 859 1621))
